newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Albright presses Vietnam on economics, rights.
newsitem.headline: Albright presses Vietnam on economics, rights.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright urged Vietnam on Friday to speed up economic reforms and improve human rights, including release of political prisoners and greater freedoms of speech, assembly and religion.
But despite these concerns, she signed a copyright pact with the government and announced she had authorised the U.S. trade and development agency to include Vietnam in its programmes.
The agency provides grants for expensive feasibility studies to U.S. firms competing for large projects.

The United States is "disappointed with the pace of economic reforms (in Vietnam)," Albright told a news conference after meetings in the capital Hanoi with Vietnamese Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam.

She called for a "Doi Moi 2", meaning a second phase of economic innovations. Vietnam launched Doi Moi ("renovation") a decade ago to reconstruct an economy laid low by socialist central planning and physical destruction from decades of war ending in 1975.

Albright later flew to Ho Chi Minh City -- known as Saigon during the Vietnam War when the United States backed South Vietnam against the communist North -- and held talks with Communist Party General Secretary Do Muoi.
She was the first secretary of state to visit the city since before the Americans lost the war in 1975.
U.S. Ambassador Pete Peterson said the stop -- and Saturday's groundbreaking for a new U.S. consulate -- was important for the American psyche and meant the United States had put the past behind.
"We're not talking 1975 anymore, we're talking 1997," said Peterson, a former prisoner of war in Vietnam.
In Hanoi, Albright told reporters she advised Vietnamese leaders they must remove barriers to trade and investment.

U.S. firms say Vietnam has been slow to enact needed reforms but at the same time has been pushing for most-favoured-nation trade benefits. It is one of only a half-dozen countries that does not have MFN status which grants lower import tariffs.

But Albright said Vietnam first has to speed issuing permits under a programme that encourages Vietnamese refugees in Thailand and Hong Kong to return home. The lure was a last chance to be considered for resettlement in the United States under liberal criteria.

Once Hanoi's cooperation improves, the U.S. Jackson-Vanik law, which demands free immigration in return for trade ties, can be waived and American firms can qualify for government loans and insurance to do business in Vietnam, Albright said.
She said she could recommend that Jackson-Vanik be waived soon, if the visa processing is accelerated. Once this is followed by a trade accord, Vietnam can qualify for MFN.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Vietnamese officials pledged their commitment to economic reforms.

On human rights, a highly sensitive issue, Albright raised the cases of three political prisoners and stressed the need for greater freedoms of speech, religion and assembly in the Southeast Asian nation.
They involved detainees Doan Viet Hoat and Nguyen Van Que and Buddhist leader Thich Quang Do.
Albright handed Cam a letter from Hoat's wife and asked him to ensure the letter was delivered and to allow the wife, who is now in the United States, to visit her husband.
Burns said Cam accepted the letter without comment but Kiet argued that the two countries have different approaches to human rights and Vietnam must be concerned about internal stability.

Albright also said she pressed Hanoi to assign more personnel to the U.S. search for Americans missing from the Vietnam War and provide greater access to archives. Burns said Kiet promised full cooperation.

The main focus of Albright's trip was economics. But her first act on Friday was to be briefed by military officers overseeing the U.S. office that searches for the 1,584 U.S. servicemen in Vietnam still unaccounted for (missing in action, or MIA) after the war.
Of that number, 196 were priority cases in January 1992 -- cases based on live sightings of individuals -- and now only 48 individuals remain on that list, military officials said.
The issue has long been an emotional one in the United States, whose society was bitterly divided by U.S. involvement in the war.
But there are increasing suggestions the intense search for missing servicemen -- costing about $10 million a year -- may one day have to end without resolving all the cases.
"I don't think you'll get 100 percent accounting," said Army Lieutenant Colonel Jonathan Chase, the chief of the search operations who briefed Albright.

Albright told reporters en route to Hanoi: "I think that for thousands of Americans the POW-MIA situation will never be resolved. It will clearly be part of the agenda and it will clearly be part of a priority issue that we keep pressing."
Still, with Vietnam a key regional economic player and political power, she said: "I think people know the importance of dealing with Vietnam as a country...we have to move ahead."
